questions.explanation: Because the write puts the source's column index into the destination's row position, the destination has one row for each column of the source, so a 3-row by 5-column grid becomes 5 rows by 3 columns. questions.topic: Counting side-sharing pairs on a board
questions.learningObjective: count adjacent cell pairs by shared boundaries rather than by degrees
questions.stem: A tile game plays on a board of 4 rows by 6 columns, where two cells are neighbours only when they share a side. Counting every neighbouring pair once rather than once per endpoint, how many neighbouring pairs does the whole board contain? Respond with the integer only.
questions.explanation: Neighbouring pairs are counted by the boundaries they share, so a 4-by-6 board has 4 * (6 - 1) = 20 pairs running across the rows and 6 * (4 - 1) = 18 pairs running down the columns, giving 38. Multiplying 4 by 6 by 4 to reach 96 is the tempting shortcut, because every cell does have four sides, but that counts each pair twice, once from each of its two cells, so a degree total always comes out at exactly double the number of pairs.
questions.hint: Count the horizontal gaps and the vertical gaps separately.

questions.topic: A safe seed for a row maximum
questions.learningObjective: choose a running-maximum seed that is no greater than any candidate in the row

options.text: int best = g[r][0];, because the scan starts from a value inside the row.

questions.explanation: A running maximum is only correct when the seed is no greater than any candidate the scan may meet, and a cell already inside the row guarantees that, so seeding from g[r][0] lets the comparison climb and the answer becomes -4 and -2. Zero is the tempting seed, because a new int[] is zero-filled and zero looks like a neutral starting value, but no value in this grid is below zero, so the seed itself survives the whole scan and the array stays [0, 0]; the negating option fails the same test in reverse, since -9 becomes 9 and beats every real candidate.

questions.topic: Totals of per-row and per-column maxima
questions.learningObjective: compare the total of the per-row maxima with the total of the per-column maxima
questions.stem: For the grid {{4, 9, 2}, {3, 8, 1}, {7, 5, 6}} the per-row maxima are [9, 8, 7] and the per-column maxima are [7, 9, 6]. What is the sum of the per-row maxima minus the sum of the per-column maxima? Respond with the integer only.
questions.explanation: The per-row maxima total 9 + 8 + 7 = 24 and the per-column maxima total 7 + 9 + 6 = 22, so the difference is 2. Expecting 0 is the tempting answer, because every one of the nine values appears exactly once among the row maxima and exactly once among the column maxima, so the two totals pick from the same multiset; the largest value happens to be both a row maximum and a column maximum, but the mid-range values land in different groups, which is where the 2 comes from.
questions.hint: Add each set of three values, then subtract the totals.
